patient_information: A 35-year-old HIV-positive Malawian woman on antiretroviral treatment for 3 years, with an unknown CD4 count.
chief_complaint: A painful ocular tumour in her left eye, leading to referral for exenteration.
history_of_present_illness: Eight months prior, she noticed a whitish lesion on her left conjunctiva, which grew bigger, turned reddish, and caused loss of eyesight in the affected eye, with increasing pain; prior treatments with non-specific and herbal eye drops were ineffective.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is from Malawi, an area where OSSN is commonly seen in HIV-positive individuals in sub-Saharan Africa; HIV infection, UV radiation, and HPV are strongly associated with OSSN.
physical_exam: Localized swelling of the left eyeball and orbit, incomplete lid closure, left preauricular lymph nodes are swollen, right eye visual acuity is 6/6, left eye has no light perception, and the rest of her physical examination is unremarkable.
labs_and_diagnostics: The CD4 count is unknown; ultrasound biomicroscopy and Toluidine blue 0.05% vital staining are mentioned as diagnostic tools for OSSN, but no results are reported for this patient.
differential_diagnosis: Advanced ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN) is the most likely diagnosis, but early stages may be confused with pterygium, amelanotic naevus, lipoma, amelanotic melanomas, lymphomas, or adenocarcinomas.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was recommended analgesic treatment with nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, counselling, and extended exenteration of the left eyeball and orbit; her HIV viral load should be checked, and her ART may be switched; she refused surgical intervention and was discharged with antibiotics and bandaging for pain control, with an offer to return.
final_diagnosis: Advanced ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN), specifically Squamous cell carcinoma of the conjunctiva (SCCC).

images.caption: Left eye with marked axial proptosis, nasal upper lid covered with tetracycline eye ointment.
Squamous cell carcinoma of the conjunctiva (SCCC). The lesion is commonly seen in HIV patients in the tropics and should not be missed during routine clinical examination.
